newsitem.title: USA: ARCO sees "dramatic" rise in production.
newsitem.headline: ARCO sees "dramatic" rise in production.

text.p: Atlantic Richfield Co (ARCO) chairman and chief executive Mike Bowlin said Monday he expects "dramatic increases" in the company's international reserves and production during the next five years.
Speaking at the annual meeting of shareholders at ARCO headquarters here, Bowlin also said he expects stable levels of U.S. production in the next five years.

Bowlin said four international projects in 1996 - one in the South China Sea, another in Algeria and two in the United Kingdom's North Sea - will add about 60,000 barrels of oil in equivalent production a day in the short term.

The Rhourde el Baguel project in Algeria could by itself add another 50,000 barrels per day net production over the next five years, he noted. The project added 218 million barrels of reserves in 1996, he added.
He said ARCO expects Venezuela's Congress to soon approve a heavy oil upgrading project which will combine ARCO's skills in upstream and downstream technologies.

In the project, ARCO will produce crude oil from the Hamaca field in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt and upgrade it for export sales, he said. Hamaca will use ARCO's refinery coking technology and experience and will enable the company to book over 300 million barrels of reserves, he said.
On gas commercialization, Bowlin said two major gas projects are on the horizon: Weriagar in eastern Indonesia and Shearwater in the North Sea.
"I believe Weriagar will prove to be one of the best exploration finds the industry has made in recent years," Bowlin said.

Although ARCO is still evaluating Weriagar, Bowlin said it would be developed as a liquefied natural gas projectm and gas from the area and adjacent structures would be sold into readily accessible Asian markets.

In the U.K.'s central North Sea, ARCO and its partners recently announced development of the Shearwater gas and condensate field for start-up in mid- 2000, he said. Shearwater will be the first development in an area that has a number of promising prospects, he said.
He noted that that ARCO's LUKARCO joint venture with the Russian oil giant LUKOIL, completed the purchase of a 5 percent interest in the Tengiz oil field.
Meanwhile, ARCO's U.S. so-called Lower 48 production is expected to grow, while new production will help stop declines in Alaska after 1999.
For example, Alpine, a 300- million barrel ARCO-operated oil field on Alaska's North Slope, will start production in 2000 and the recently discovered Tam field may start production in 1998, he said.
